extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and scientific classification (those learning to form and evaluate definitions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming and evaluating definitions of names and attributes in logic and science, covering complete vs. imperfect definitions, modes of definition, and the relation between definitions and factual postulates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as declaration of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest and most correct notion of a Definition is, a proposition declaratory of the meaning of a word; namely, either the meaning which it bears in common acceptation, or that which the speaker or writer, for the particular purposes of his discourse, intends to annex to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A definition should state the connotation (the attributes) that the term denotes. It is a proposition about the use/meaning of a name; if a name has no meaning (e.g., a proper name) it is unsusceptible of definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete (philosophical) definition — full connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a name, according to this view, is the sum total of all the essential propositions which can be framed with that name for their subject. All propositions the truth of which is implied in the name, all those which we are made aware of by merely hearing the name, are included in the definition, if complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete definition must enable the derivation of all truths implied by the name without other premises. It may be long but is the most precise and least equivocal form. Treat definition as analysis: resolve a complex meaning into constituent attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs indirect modes of definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct mode: explicitly state 'Man is a name connoting such and such attributes.' The indirect mode: predicate of the name other name(s) of known signification which connote the same aggregation of attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct definitions are precise but verbose and technical; indirect (using synonymous or composite connotative names) are briefer and more usual in common discourse. Using other names is acceptable provided they together exactly express the connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of single-attribute (abstract) names
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract name connotes only a single attribute (e.g., 'white' or 'rational'), one must look to the foundation phenomenon for definition; analyze the phenomenon (its parts, causes, effects) to define the attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the attribute grounds in a complex phenomenon, dissect cause and effect to produce a definition (e.g., 'eloquence' = power of influencing the feelings by speech/writing). If the foundation is a simple feeling lacking analysable parts, definition may require appeal to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of simple feelings can be indefinable in words
rubrics_metrics.description: The only names which are unsusceptible of definition, because their meaning is unsusceptible of analysis, are the names of the simple feelings themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such names cannot be unfolded by words and require direct appeal to the personal experience of the individual addressed (e.g., sensation of white). They occupy a similar status to proper names in this respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential but incomplete definitions (practical adequacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ordinary definitions state only part of the connotation (a part sufficient to mark out the denotation). Such 'essential but incomplete' definitions may be adequate as long as the enumerated attributes suffice to distinguish known instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are common and serviceable: e.g., 'Man is a rational animal' — not a full analysis but practical for current usage. Beware: they are liable to be overturned by discovery of new objects (they’re provisional).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental definitions or descriptions (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions formed by attributes not part of the connotation (accidents) are termed Descriptions and are rejected by logicians as genuine definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive definitions may still discriminate correctly (convertible with the name) and thus be pragmatically useful; but they are not philosophically genuine because they don't derive from the essence. Example anti-patterns: defining 'man' by 'featherless biped' or 'who cooks his food' without connecting to essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convertibility/coextensiveness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct (even if accidental) definition must be convertible with the name which it professes to define; that is, it should be exactly co-extensive with it, predicable of every object of which the name is predicable and of nothing else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the test of adequacy for descriptive or imperfect definitions: if the description is predicable precisely for the same things as the name, it functions correctly for discrimination and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per genus et differentiam (and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical rule: the definition of a species should be per genus et differentiam (genus plus difference). But Mill notes differentia is often only part of constitutive peculiarities and that a truly complete definition would require all differentiæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genus+difference form is rhetorically useful but not strictly necessary for all cases (e.g., summum genus lacks a superior genus). Use genus+all differentiæ where possible; recognise the classical formula's pragmatic rather than absolute force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special/technical definitions for classificatory purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: For scientific or special purposes a common name may be given a special connotation (without altering denotation) so it can be defined to serve classification (e.g., Cuvier’s 'man' as mammiferous animal having two hands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such technical definitions are genuine within their intended classificatory scheme. The purpose is often classification rather than purely expounding ordinary meaning; always indicate the special purpose/context when using them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific definitions are progressive and provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions change as classifications and knowledge advance; the attributes connoted by a term in science can recede or grow with discovery (example: the term 'acid').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and permit modification of scientific definitions over time. Do not treat scientific definitions as immutable; they serve as landmarks for classification and will evolve with theory and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions from postulates (definitions do not assert existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a real distinction between definitions of names and propositions that covertly assert the existence of things. A definition is a nominal proposition stating meaning; any covert assertion that a thing exists with those properties is a postulate, not part of the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a definition as a factual premise in reasoning unless you separately assert existence. Example: Euclidean 'definition' of circle contains a postulate that such a figure may be described; proofs rely on that postulate, not on the nominal definition alone. Avoid drawing factual conclusions solely from definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic conclusions only from definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: From a definition (considered as a declaration of meaning) one can only validly infer propositions about the meanings of words; one cannot validly infer factual claims about the world (unless a postulate of existence is added).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware syllogisms that treat definitional clauses as factual premises — they may be formally valid but their conclusions about reality will be unwarranted. Example anti-pattern: deriving 'some serpents breathe flame' from definitional premises about dragons without asserting dragons' real existence.
